newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's medics persist in strikes over wages.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's medics persist in strikes over wages.

text.p: Serbia's doctors, nurses and social workers said on Monday they would keep up their protests after the government failed to meet its promise to pay late wages by the end of last week.

"There will be no further negotiations with the government. The strike will be intensified and we will work at minimum levels," Stevan Djordjevic, president of the Serbian health and social workers trade union, told reporters.
Health and social workers throughout Serbia have been on strike since May 12 over unpaid wages and neglect of the sector, providing only a skeleton service.

The doors of the biggest out-patient clinic in Belgrade were closed for the first time on Monday as the strike entered its sixth week, with only chemotherapy, dialysis and kidney transplant patients allowed in.
Despite prior announcements of its closure, some 500 people gathered outside, venting their anger on striking staff.
"All our lives contributions for health have been deducted from our wages and now when we need it, we cannot get medical assistance," a pensioner shouted.
Djordjevic said it was easier for people to blame doctors and nurses. "But we will not be blackmailed by those who say our jobs are so important they do not allow us not to work."
A Serbian health ministry official has said the government was unable to meet the deadline due to "lack of funds from real sources", but promised payments would start this week.
Djordjevic vowed the trade union would persist until the state met its obligations.
Doctors and nurses said they would block streets outside their institutions for an hour each day in an effort to draw more attention to their protest.
Of Serbia's 24,000 doctors, 60,000 nursing staff and 40,000 other employees in the sector, 70 percent are on strike.

Serbia has been rocked by a wave of blue and white collar strikes over the past few months as the government, strapped for cash but committed to tight fiscal policy, delayed paying out wages and pensions.
Opposition parties have accused the government of using the strikes to channel bitterness at overall impoverishment and economic recession away from itself to the health sector.
Clinics throughout Serbia are in dire straits, with no medicines, supplies, equipment or food.

"Patients get 100 grams of bread and tea for breakfast, potatoes or cabbage for lunch, 100 grams of bread and 200 ml of milk for dinner," Miljka Kacarevic, a senior nurse and member of the strike committee, told Reuters.
Although some patients left hospital beds on Monday to join protesting medical staff outside the Serbian government building, the strike has not attracted wider attention.
